en: Having prostrated before that Buddha, the knower of the true path, who demonstrated to humans and gods the way to the pacification of the cause of suffering, I shall compose this treatise, the *Abhidharmadīpa*. 1.1.
If the *sattva* and other [guṇas] do not undergo change, it follows that there would be an absence of manifestation;
furthermore, because of their modification, the *prakṛti* itself would be subject to change, since it is non-different from them.
Karma does not exist because it has been relinquished by its own nature; nor do the stains consist of a cognizable or manifest self-nature.
In the first case, there would be an absence of liberation; in the second, there would be other afflictions as well.
The aggregate of form consists of the ten bases and elements beginning with the eye;
the three aggregates designated as "dharmas" consist of [the remaining] three aggregates, along with non-informative matter and the three eternal factors.
The other seven consciousness-elements, which are designated as "mind," are also [included].
For an *āyatana* is defined as a door of arrival (*āyadvāra*), while a *dhātu* is defined as a lineage (*gotra*). 5.

The Sage taught the twelve bases (āyatana) because they are conducive to yoga and formlessness, and he taught the eighteen elements (dhātu) for the sake of abandoning the notion of the unity of consciousness and so forth. 6.
Because the six [senses] are mutually dependent, that which is their cause is indeed the mind (*manas*).
Because it serves as the basis for both the material and the immaterial, the five [senses] are designated as "material" (*rūpin*).
The inclusion of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) within their own nature is traditionally taught;
likewise, the equality of mind and mental factors is due to their never being separated from their own nature.

One who is proficient in the method of the treatise should state the inclusion within these very [categories] of those others mentioned in other sūtras, having considered their specific characteristics through the intellect. (Abhidh-d 9)
The mutual inclusion of the aggregates (skandha) and so forth should be understood according to their respective natures;
there is no inclusion within the aggregates of eternal things, because they do not fall [into the past] and so on across the time periods.
The inclusion of even the eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma should be understood as occurring precisely within these [categories], because they lead one to enter upon the true path. (Abhidh-d 11)
The measure of the *dharmaskandhas* is the individual exposition of each [topic] such as the truths;
however, some maintain that their true nature consists of speech, while others hold it to be names. *Abhidharmadīpa* 12.
The six fundamental elements are considered the basis for the designation of a "sentient being"; it is said that through their differentiation, the conceit "I am" (asmimāna) ceases. Abhidh-d_13.
Indeed, consciousness at the moment of birth should be understood as being exclusively afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), because it is the basis for rebirth.
The element of space (*khadhātu*) is distinct from [the derived] space, because it is included within the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*).
Space is indeed the cause proximate to the element of space;
these [elements] are the causes of derived matter, and that [derived matter] is the cause of the mind. (Abhidh-d 15)

That which functions as direct perception, that which grasps even what has not yet been reached, that which reaches objects further away than others, and that which is more proficient than the rest— [these are the characteristics of the visual faculty].
The first category [of dharmas] is "visible"; ten are "material" and "possessing resistance.
With the exception of visible form and sound, those same [ten] are considered "indeterminate."

The remaining [elements] are all of three kinds here; in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are fourteen, excluding the elements of taste and odor along with their corresponding consciousnesses, and the last three [elements].
The last three are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*); the remaining ones are with-outflows.
The first five have an object (*sālambana*); the [last] three are [also] figurative (*sopacāra*), being of three kinds.
The [mental] faculty has as its own object qualities that are non-conceptual, because it does not involve recollection and does not involve discernment.
Recollection belongs to the mental level; the first [of these two types of mental consciousness] is non-discerning, while the second is discerning.

In the desire realm, the fivefold group of consciousnesses is accompanied by one [type of] conceptualization; other than those, [the mental consciousness] is accompanied by three. In the first dhyāna, that which is non-concentrated is likewise [accompanied by three].
By two [faculties], it is undistracted; by one, it is based on the eye, ear, and body;
by two, it is distracted above that; and by one alone, it is concentrated.
For one whose seeds of merit have been severed,
there is no wholesome consciousness with conceptualization, except for that which pertains to rebirth.

For a fool who is free from passion for sense-pleasures and possesses the nature of non-decline, there is no unwholesome state of either kind; nor does the noble one possess the highest afflicted state.
Nothing that is non-afflicted and neutral has conceptualization of a higher level as its object;
nor does anything afflicted or conceptual have a lower level as its sphere of activity. (Abhidharmadīpa 25)
For an Āryan who still possesses attachment and is endowed with wholesome roots, two [types of death] occur in three realms;
however, in the second dhyāna and above, there is neither wholesome nor afflicted death, as these are not seen there.

Due to application, the proximity of its constituent factors, and the homogeneity of the mental continuum, memory arises in the mind regarding an object previously experienced by consciousness. (Abhidharmadīpa 27)
Due to the opposite of this— namely, dullness and being overwhelmed by the disease of the afflictions—
forgetfulness arises regarding things previously known.

That which is seen by a mind of two, three, four, or five types is remembered by that same mind and by others; however, in the destruction of the vision of obstacles, one does not remember what was seen by another.
Regarding the five consciousnesses, that which is experienced by one is also remembered by another, and indeed by the others as well. (Abhidharmadīpa 30)

In this context, that mind which has experienced two types of neutral [states], such as the twelve [factors] and so forth, is remembered by means of exactly eight [mental applications], because of the exclusion of those belonging to the formless realm and the obscured-neutral states of the form realm. *Abhidharmadīpa* 31.

But that which is remembered by means of the obscured-unwholesome and the wholesome states pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness, respectively—excluding the two types of neutral states pertaining to the desire realm—is remembered by ten [mental applications]. (Abhidharmadīpa 32)
In the realm of form (rūpa), however, that which was seen by the non-obscured neutral [mind] is remembered again by other [minds],
excluding the two types of neutral minds in the formless realm (ārūpya).
The knowledge of the neutral states of the formless realm is known by nine [minds];
that which belongs to the desire realm excludes the two neutral states, and likewise excludes the obscured-unspecified state of the form realm.
The seven [mental factors] called "mind" have an object; that which is called "dharmas" is associated [with them].
Those that are formless, together with sound, are non-appropriated; these nine are of two kinds.
The tangible is of two kinds: those that share its characteristics (sadharmāṃśa) and the nine derivative material elements (bhautika).
These ten possess parts (sāvayava), are corporeal (mūrta), and these same ten are accumulated (saṃcita).
Visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility are considered to consist of that which cuts and that which is cut;
they are also that which burns and weighs, or else they are that which is burned and weighed. *Abhidharmadīpa* 37.
The five material sense-faculties consist of both maturation and accumulation;
the immaterial [faculties] are not accumulative. The remaining [factors] are of three kinds, and sound is of two kinds.
The eye and its perception may be attained either separately or together.
The twelve internal [bases] are to be known, as well as the six external ones consisting of the objects.
The last three [faculties] are of three kinds; the remaining ones are abandoned through the path of cultivation.
There is no form to be abandoned by seeing, nor is there anything undefiled or non-conceptual [to be so abandoned].
That which is called "dharma" is exclusively homogeneous (sabhāga); the remaining [elements] are recorded as being of both kinds.
It is considered homogeneous when it possesses its own activity within the state of being homogeneous with that [object]. Abhidh-d_41.
The eye and a portion of the dharma-element are said to be vision in nine ways;
the wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not vision because it lacks investigative judgment.
Just as the eye perceives visible objects during both cloudy and cloudless nights and days,
so too do the defiled and undefiled visions of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) perceive their objects.
The eye sees; consciousness cognizes its own object-domain.
Because one is characterized by mere observation and the other by apprehension, there is a very great distinction between the two.
The function of consciousness arises from either one eye or from both;
the mind, the eye, and the ear do not reach their objects, whereas the other three [senses] do so otherwise.
Those [cognitions] that grasp without reaching [the object] are established because they perceive both distant and near objects simultaneously;
if it is argued that this is like the light of a lamp and so forth, we say no, because that light arises simultaneously [with its source].
If it is argued that [the soul] would follow after all objects of perception, we say no, because of the observation of magnets and the like;
if it is argued that there is no fault because of its omnipresence, we say no, because that is illogical, as in the case of sesame oil.
For above the eye there is neither body nor form, nor is there mind born of the sense-organ;
however, the object of the eye and that [eye] itself are entirely present for the consciousness and for the body respectively.
Above the ear there is no body, no sound, and no one's own mind;
yet there is the resonance of consciousness, and those two [body and sound] exist for the body everywhere.
For the three [senses], all three [realms] are their own; for the body, consciousness is also of the lower [realm];
the mind is indeterminate; thus has the manifold nature of the yogi been demonstrated.
Those aggregates which are designated as "appropriation" (upādāna), whether they are with-outflows (sāsrava) or without-outflows (anāsrava),
should be known as exclusively with-outflows, because they perform the function of assisting those [outflows] and so forth.
The synonyms for the aggregates (skandha) begin with "time" (adhvan), while those for the existing entity (vastu) begin with "phenomena" (dharma).
However, those which are designated as "with outflows" (sāsrava) are spoken of by the names of "suffering" (duḥkha) and so forth.
Because their objects, self-natures, and functions are one, they constitute a single element (*dhātu*);
yet, although there are two [physical organs] such as the eyes, they arise as two due to the threefold nature of their activity.
Due to its uncommon excellence, its sovereignty, and its being internal,
cognition is distinguished by these [qualities], even though there are multiple causes.

Because it is eternal and wholesome, Nirvana is truly a substantial entity; since it is a substance consisting of the core essence, the single dharma called "Nirvana" is considered to possess substantial reality.
The first stainless mind is called a "moment" (kṣaṇa) due to its rarity;
because of that wondrous moment, these latter three are termed "momentary" (kṣaṇika).
The nose, the tongue, and the body—these three are equal in that they grasp objects of their own kind;
the basis for the last one is past, as is the case for the [other] five together with them.
Relying indeed upon the preparatory stage (anāgamya) or else upon the four dhyānas,
the eye-element is ceased by means of the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga).
The fragrance element ceases by relying on the *anāgamya* [dhyāna];
the mind element [ceases] either by relying on the *anāgamya* or by relying on the seven [stages].
The preliminary concentration (anāgamya) and likewise the first [dhyāna] are designated as "eye-consciousness" and so forth;
one should explain them according to their application due to the manifold nature of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
For by fully understanding the eye-element as belonging to the realm of form, an ordinary person attains detachment from the entire realm consisting of form.
Therefore, from that element of latent dispositions (anuśaya), he abandons thirty-one;
yet at that time, he does not eliminate any of the fetters (saṃyojana).
When he attains detachment from the realm of form and abandons the three underlying tendencies,
then that noble one completely exhausts no further fetter whatsoever.
But by thoroughly understanding the element of eye-consciousness,
and by thoroughly understanding that very [element], one necessarily becomes dispassionate toward the Brahma-world.
But at that time, that ordinary person (pṛthagjana), while fully understanding the odor-element and what is called the taste-element, does not exhaust any fetter whatsoever.
One attains detachment from sensual desires and certainly abandons even the latent tendencies;
at that time, one casts off the thirty-six [defilements], the three fetters, and the [remaining] bonds.
The noble one, however, effects detachment from desire regarding the latent dispositions as well;
he fully understands four [fetters] and also completely abandons three.
Fully understanding the mind-element, one becomes detached from the formless realms;
one abandons three underlying tendencies and likewise fully masters the triad.
Indeed, by fully understanding that very joy, he abandons it;
he attains detachment from the Ābhāsvara realm, yet he does not destroy the outflows (āsravas).
Fully understanding that pleasure, the yogi abandons it both here and now;
he attains detachment from the Śubhakṛtsna realm, yet he does not destroy the afflictions.
The five qualities are cognizable by two [faculties]; all [factors], both perishable and imperishable, are causes.
With the exception of half of the dharma-realm, the six external [objects] do not have the nature of sense-faculties.
The characteristics, etymologies, and other attributes of the entire twenty-two-fold section on the faculties will be stated here in brief.
By name there are twenty-two, but by substance they are seventeen;
for the two [types of sensation] are not other than the three groups of nine, beginning with pleasure, which are produced from their respective causes.
Because the characteristic of a thorn does not exist [in them], yet the name "thorn" remains meaningful,
others maintain that even though these three belong to the category of the three [types of suffering], they are understood as having a specific meaning.
Because they are the cause of a distinguished cognition and because of their specific predominance,
the two [faculties] are distinguished from the body-faculty, just like the eye-faculty and the others.
The wise declare that the object of the senses has sovereignty as its purpose:
for the five [senses], it is the manifestation of their own respective objects; for four of them, however, it is the two types of objects.
Others understand sovereignty (*īśitva*) as the apprehension of one's own object-domain and so forth;
others who consider themselves wise say it is simply the cognition of one's own object. (Abhidh-d 77)

The sequence [of the faculties] is established because of the arising of afflictions, the attainment of qualities such as faith and so forth, and the purity resulting from the accumulation of the fruits and the defilements. (Abhidharmadīpa 78)
That which is designated as "sentient being," the diversity of sentient beings, steadfastness, the arising of afflictions,
the means for the path, and the attainment of the fruit— these are considered to be the nature of the faculties (indriyatā).
There are fourteen [faculties] because they are the basis for contact, its arising, its support, and its enjoyment;
the other eight are faculties because they are the causes of heaven and liberation.

The Sage did not declare desire to be a faculty because it is a constituent part of vigor; nor contact, because it merely nourishes experience; nor perception, because it is overcome by wisdom. Abhidh-d_81 //

In the purification of faith and the other [faculties], as well as in the arising of their defilements, attention (manaskāra) is declared to be the primary factor, not the faculty (indriya). Abhidh-d_82 //
Because it conforms to expectation, resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is also not a faculty;
because of the doubt regarding the production of a fruit at another time, volition (*cetanā*) is not [a faculty] either.
Nor is this heedfulness [attained] through vigor alone, nor is it shame due to the restraint of audacity;
nor is it equanimity, nor even non-attachment, because they are overwhelmed by vigor and faith.
Pliancy is not [an attainment] because of the intensity of its feeling; nor are the outflows [attainments] because they are censurable.
Birth and the other [conditioned factors] are not [attainments] because they exist for the sake of another; Nirvana is not [an attainment] because it is devoid of activity.

Bodily affliction is physical suffering (*duḥkha*), while mental distress is mental suffering (*daurmanasya*). Happiness (*sukha*) and cheerfulness (*sumanastā*) are both physical and mental pleasure (*sāta*). *Abhidharmadīpa* 86.
Due to its excellence, mental pleasure is sometimes described as *sukha*.
In the six stages, the faculties beginning with the dustless (*nīrajaska*) are to be known;
the others, however, are to be seen as stainless (*nirmala*) faculties belonging to the nine stages.
Mental dissatisfaction (daurmanasya) is to be abandoned by two [means]; the three mental feelings are of three kinds;
nine are to be abandoned by cultivation; five are of two kinds, but not the three.
In the desire realm, two types of maturation are obtained through those arising in succession from the past;
by others, six, seven, or eight; but in the form realm, six; while in the final [formless] realm, only the life-faculty.
In the death-moment, three are ceased; in the intermediate state, eight;
in the desire realm, ten, eight, nine, four, or five wholesome [dharmas] are ceased.
The attainment of the beginning and the end is by nine [faculties]; that of the two middles is by seven or eight;
and the attainment of the final fruit is by eleven, through the process of abandonment.
The thorough knowledge of one's own element is by way of the perspective of its own opposite.
The full comprehension of the desire realm (kāmadhātu-parijñāna) is generally held to be by means of seven [knowledges];
however, it is said to be by means of eight objects, both with and without outflows (sāsrava and anāsrava).
The full comprehension of the form realm (rūpadhātu) is held to be by means of ten faculties;
the full comprehension of the final realm (the formless realm) is said to be by means of eleven.
All sentient beings dwelling in the three realms are endowed with equanimity, vitality, and the mental faculty;
those in the desire realm possess the skin, femininity, and the male organs, while those in the form realm possess the eye and the other [senses].
Indeed, one who possesses desire [is affected] by suffering; one who possesses passion for that [realm] by mental distress;
one born in the higher realms by pleasure; and likewise the Noble One (ārya) by the "wholesome" (śubha), while those below are likewise [affected by the unwholesome].
Through joy and light, he arises from the lower [realms]; by means of the auspicious, he is rooted in the auspicious.
Those on the path of training (śaikṣa) abide on the path to liberation; the non-trainee (aśaikṣa), the Arhat, proceeds upon his own path.
One who possesses equanimity, life-force, or mind is necessarily endowed with three;
one who possesses bodily pleasure or the eye is endowed with four, and likewise one who possesses the [other] five.
One endowed with the female faculty and so forth possesses eight; one who experiences suffering possesses seven;
one possessing the last two [faculties] possesses eleven; and one possessing the first six [faculties] possesses seven or six.
Those born in the three continents or in the hells, even if fixed in falsehood,
are endowed with many— up to nineteen— or with few, as few as eight.
Those in the intermediate state, hungry ghosts, animals, and those who follow through faith are endowed with either thirteen or nineteen [faculties].
Those who are fixed in rightness and those who are liberated through faith are endowed with eleven [faculties], or with ten, or with nine.
The Arhats known as those liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), the body-witnesses (kāyasākṣin), and those called both [liberated by wisdom and by concentration],
possess eleven faculties, or alternatively, eighteen.
The gods of the desire realm die after a short time—ten [kalpas] plus seven;
they are endowed with nineteen faculties when they possess many [faculties].
But those born in the two dhyānas possess, at the very minimum, ten faculties plus five;
the Śubhakṛtsna gods are endowed with ten plus four.
For the Bṛhatphala gods are endowed with only the very few thirteen [faculties],
whereas these [Akaniṣṭha gods] are possessed of all sixteen, which are the most numerous of faculties.
The formless realms possess eight, ten, and eleven [faculties] respectively, being small, medium, and great;
sentient beings, including the gods of the desire realm, are endowed with thirteen.
One who is devoid of virtue is endowed with eight, or with ten—that is, three more—or with the last two [faculties] in small measure; at most, however, one is endowed with twenty-one.
An external atom is inseparable from seven substances;
in the realm of desire, it is increased by one in the body and increased by two in the eye and other [senses].
In the same way, it should be understood that [the objects] are of such a nature, excluding the pair of odor and taste;
for the mind, together with mental factors, is conditioned by its own specific characteristics.
The ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) are: discernment, perception, volition, mindfulness, desire, contact, resolve, wisdom, concentration, and attention. Abhidh-d_112.
Faith, heedfulness, non-negligence, pliancy, moral shame,
dread of blame, the roots, vigor, and non-harming— these are known as the ten wholesome mental factors.

Styāna (sloth), pramāda (heedlessness), āśraddhya (lack of faith), ālasya (laziness), mūḍhi (delusion), and auddhatya (restlessness)—these six [mental factors] are present in the defiled; however, in the unwholesome, there are two: āhrīkya (lack of shame) and anapatrāpya (lack of dread).
Deceit, guile, intoxication, anger, harmfulness, envy, malice, subtle resentment, and avarice—these ten are the ground of the minor afflictions. *Abhidharmadīpa* 115.
Just as a substance such as earth is distinguished by various words through its connection with qualities like blue, so too is the mind [distinguished] through its connection with mental factors.
Just as the diversity of the primary elements and their derivatives is produced by their own nature and activity,
so too should the distinctness of the mind and mental factors be understood.
Just as a transformation is perceived in water due to its connection with something related to it,
so too should the modification of the mind be observed due to its association with that which is associated with it.
"Quality," "qualifier," "attribute," "measure-occurrence," and likewise "substratum"—words such as these function in dependence upon a primary referent. *Abhidharmadīpa* 119.
Among these, the mind is primary because it grasps the mere object and so forth;
it is also the seed for the various processes of both purity and defilement.
The mind belonging to the realm of desire arises together with twelve factors; it is undefiled and neutral, like the sun with its rays. *Abhidharmadīpa* 121.
Likewise, the mind arises as obscured by eighteen [mental states];
however, together with twenty-two, the mental state necessarily becomes wholesome.

An unwholesome mind arises together with twenty mental factors; that which is associated solely with delusion regarding the [four] truths should be stated as having more when accompanied by anger and so forth. *Abhidharmadīpa* 123.
Since torpor (middha) occurs everywhere, one should specify it wherever it may be present;
likewise, one should count regret (kaukṛtya) as an additional factor in some cases.
In the form realm, the unwholesome, as well as torpor and remorse, do not exist;
furthermore, in the intermediate dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) is absent, and in the stages above that, sustained thought (*vicāra*) is also absent.
The associated formation is that which possesses fivefold equality;
the dissociated formation is to be understood as that which lacks such equality.
Because there is no existence of distinct [entities], there is no over-extension regarding those possessing form;
and because of the inclusion of "conditioned phenomena" (saṃskāra), it does not follow [that the definition applies] to space and the other [unconditioned elements].

The dissociated formations (saṃskāra-viprayukta) beginning with acquisition (prāpti) are thirteen; their characteristic mark will be stated as the authoritative word of the Master and their own activity. Abhidh-d 128.
Attainment, possession, acquisition, the state of possessing dharmas, and establishment.
And [the acquisition] of those consisting of hearing and reflection, as well as of the two meditative attainments.

But for those [wholesome] dharmas accompanied by outflows (*sāsrava*) that have never before been cultivated and are free from afflictions (*niḥkleśa*), their initial acquisition is held to be threefold: simultaneously with them, prior to them, or subsequent to them.
The [minds] other than those—namely, the afflicted and the wholesome—are considered to be of three kinds;
likewise, the obscured-unspecified [minds] and the minds of emanation and knowledge are also [of three kinds].
Regarding the attainment of Nirvāṇa from the beginning, it is held that while one [aspect] is eternal and always present, the other two—
the unborn and the present— are each considered to be threefold.
That which is the cause for sentient beings’ shared inclination toward the same object is *sabhāgatā*.
*Āsaṃjñika* is the maturation [result] which consists in the cessation of mind among those who possess perception.

The attainment of the perception of the imperturbable (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) occurs in the final dhyāna; it obstructs the mind because it proceeds from a desire for liberation. It is not attained by a noble one (ārya), and it is acquired through preparatory effort (prayoga).

That which is called cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), however, should be understood as belonging to a noble one who is pure and desires to emerge from the peak of existence; it is attained through preparatory effort, is of two types of retribution, and is considered indeterminate.
Because of the absence of the four types of consciousness, because of scripture,
and because of logical reasoning, this state devoid of mind is established through the cessation of the mental state characterized by feeling.
The subsistence of vitality, consciousness, and heat is the basis for the designation of "rebirth-state" (gati);
it is held to exist as a substantial entity (dravyataḥ) both according to scripture and through reasoning.
Birth, duration, decay, and destruction—these four are the characteristics of the conditioned.
There are four [reasons] why duration is not included: because its non-existence would result in the non-establishment of its status as a cause and so forth.
The establishment of decay follows from the loss of power; it is not due to being something else, for that would imply transformation.
The loss of power is established through the cessation of a single causal function.
Since [destruction] occurs when there is birth, because it follows from the destruction of substance and activity,
and because of scripture and logical reasoning, destruction also has a cause.

Those three, beginning with names (nāma), are traditionally taught as having their birth dependent on speech-sounds, performing the function of conveying their own meanings, and possessing other names such as "designation" (saṃjñā) and so forth.

Other [factors] such as names (nāman) and so forth are to be understood as impermanent, because they reveal objects not yet reached [by the senses] through sound, and because they manifest their objects in dependence [on other conditions].
A word that makes its own form known, as well as the phonemes and so forth, certainly conveys meaning; it is by way of figurative designation (*bhakti*) that it is called such by the wise.
Because it has the nature of atoms, the oneness of sound is not tenable;
its identity [with atoms] follows from its resistance, and its establishment is through obstruction and so forth.
No eternal word called *sphoṭa* is established as distinct from sound;
because it occurs sequentially, no meaning whatsoever is expressed by such a [supposed] word.
A sound is not heard by means of hearing, nor is there any other way for hearing to function;
whoever should say otherwise would be held in derision by the wise.
These [qualities] are to be illustrated as appropriate, being both determinate and indeterminate;
because of the manifestation of their determinateness, it is understood that the Buddha is omniscient.
Those termed "sentient beings" belong to the realms of desire and form; they are outflowing and neutral, as well as maturation-born. Likewise, there is similarity, and acquisitions are of two kinds.
According to the Sūtra, because there is an absence of calamities involving sentient beings, there is no [impermanence] in the fourth [dhyāna];
since the equality of the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) is not subject to destruction, how could there be impermanence?
Seven [destructions] occur by means of fire and one by water; when seven [cycles] by water have passed, there is again a final cycle of seven by fire, and after that, the destruction by wind.
From the seven [deities] of the Āgneya group, one [is born]; immediately thereafter is Pāvanīki.
Thus, from the very grasping of life-span, there is the fueling of the Śubhakṛtsna lifespan.
Because they share the same characteristics as the humors such as wind (*vāta*), they destroy sentient beings;
due to this internal similarity, the destruction of the earth is not considered a *bhū-saṃvartanī* (earth-destruction).
Karma is held to be the cause of the births of sentient beings, the producer of both misfortune and prosperity, and the creator of the diversity of the world.
Action of the body, that which consists of speech, and that which is called mental volition—these are the actions of the world; they are the cause, not Īśvara and the like.
Because of their manifold nature, because of their sequential arising, and because it would follow that other things are likewise [dependent],
there is no dependence on anything else for the union of austerity, due to faults such as the abandonment of one's own thesis.
The power of karmas is awakened by means of ritual injunctions, time, the planets, and so forth; therefore, the designation of those [factors] as "karma" is employed through a figurative application.
In the past, informative and non-informative [action], as well as volition, constitute mental action.
Just as food is utterly consumed by fire and a cooking pot is likewise ruined,
so too is the ethical conduct of one whose mind is wounded by malice, envy, and the like, and who possesses wrong views.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth, monkhood is endowed with both conventional and true vision;
however, through convention alone, it exists when there is only one [of these], and when neither is present, it does not exist in either way.
The primary designation for the word "Buddha" applies to knowledge that is free from afflictions;
it should be understood that the secondary designation applies both to its basis and to its fruit.
Because it is eternal and pure, and because all misfortunes have ceased therein,
Dharma is likewise called Nirvana according to the primary conceptualization.
The noble ones, the qualities of the disciples, and likewise the Saṃgha from the perspective of ultimate truth—
whosoever goes for refuge to these three, he goes for refuge to the Triple Gem.
Sexual misconduct is [the most blameworthy] because it is censured by the virtuous and results in non-attainment in the next life;
false speech is the most sinful; and drinking intoxicants [is grave] because it causes the loss of mindfulness.
The [discipline] born of desire is obtained from all present [actions], whether they be of two kinds;
however, those consisting of cultivation are obtained from the fundamental [actions] of the three times.
Restraint is [taken] from all classes of sentient beings by means of the limbs and the causes;
it is not [taken] from all the limbs of restraint nor from all sentient beings by means of the causes.
The acquisition of non-restraint occurs through action or through formal undertaking;
the [acquisition of] non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) other than that [restraint or non-restraint] arises from the distinction of the field, the factors, and so forth.
The abandonment of the restraint pertaining to the desire realm occurs through the renunciation of the training and so forth;
some say it also occurs through the [four] defeats, while others say it does not, because that [reasoning] is inconsistent.
The substance of the cloth does not perish due to the destruction of its threads;
the mention of their destruction regarding the yarns serves another purpose, as in the case of [accusations of] envy, deceit, and so forth.
Due to the disappearance of the True Dharma, through the transition between other [realms], and through not obtaining what was previously unobtained,
as well as by moving to another level or by falling away, the merit born of meditative absorption is abandoned.
Likewise, noble non-material [attainment] is lost through the acquisition of a fruit, the loss of the faculties, or death;
whereas non-restraint is lost through the acquisition of self-control, the relinquishing of life, and so forth.
Non-informative matter (avijñapti), however, is intermediate; it is severed by the interruption of the force of the mind and so forth.
That which is called wholesome belonging to the desire realm is [severed] by three causes, such as the cutting off of the roots [of merit] and the rest.
Through the arising of the counteragent, the afflicted [states] belonging to the three realms are abandoned.
All [are abandoned] in the desire realm; two in the form realm; and one in the formless realm, by way of acquisition.
Action that yields a desirable fruit is declared to be wholesome (*kuśala*);
by the opposite [it is] unwholesome (*akuśala*), and other than these, it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

The first type of merit belonging to the desire realm is non-meritorious, being unwholesome by nature; that which belongs to the higher stages is "imperturbable" (āneñya), because it does not shake with respect to its maturation.
Wholesome karma is to be experienced as pleasure up to the fourth dhyāna;
elsewhere it is to be experienced as equanimity, whereas unwholesome karma is to be experienced as suffering.
Even below [the fourth dhyāna], there is intermediate karma, because of the attainment of nirvāṇa even in the last [dhyāna];
and because of the desire for three simultaneous ripenings, due to the ripening of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Furthermore, karma is fourfold, distinguished as that to be experienced in the present life and so forth;
by three of these types, a birth is projected, excluding that which is called "to be experienced in the present life."
Furthermore, all four [types of karma] project [rebirth] everywhere except in the hells;
for there, because there is an absence of desirable results, only the auspicious [karma] ripens.
In that [realm], an ordinary person who is detached from it has created karma to be experienced upon rebirth;
a stable noble one does not create other [karma] there, nor does an unstable noble one create it in the two roots of existence.
When an action is repeatedly practiced with a mind that is either afflicted or fierce,
and when it is performed toward a "good field," its fruit is determined.
Due to the excellence of the field and the intention, the fruit ripens immediately;
and for one who has just emerged from cessation [samāpatti], there is the performance of action with immediate temporal fruit.
One should know that karma which does not arise again in that same plane, and which is fixed as to its maturation, is karma that bears fruit in this very life; such is the completing karma.
The maturation of wholesome [karma] that is without investigation is exclusively mental feeling;
however, the bodily feeling resulting from karma to be experienced as suffering is desired [to be the maturation].
That which is unwholesome is black with its maturation; that which is born of form is white with its maturation.
In the realm of desire, the wholesome and unwholesome are both twofold [in terms of maturation]; that which is stainless effects the abandonment of those two.

The four paths of seeing constitute the path of vision; the paths of uninterrupted continuity in the realm of desire constitute the path of cultivation. This [path] effects the destruction of black karma.
But that volition which exists in the ninth [path of liberation] destroys both black and black-white karma;
however, for white karma, it exists in the paths of immediate succession within each dhyāna.
All unwholesome karma of body and so forth is considered misconduct (*duścarita*);
likewise, the three beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) constitute the threefold mental misconduct.
That which is auspicious, beginning with non-covetousness and so forth, is called the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*).
This consists of two fundamental karmas; these ten paths of action are both auspicious and inauspicious.
The six [types of] unmanifest [action] produced by [volition] are of two natures; those six are also made [into] one.
The seven virtuous [unmanifest actions] are to be known as being of two kinds, while those that are concentrated are of one kind.
That which is non-informative (avijñapti) in the preliminary stages (sāmantaka) is the reverse in the subsequent stages (pṛṣṭha).
The preparatory effort (prayoga), however, arises from the three roots; covetousness and the others arise from the three roots.
Wholesome [actions] consist of the preliminary and subsequent stages, and they arise from the three roots of wholesomeness.
Killing, harsh speech, and malice are accomplished through hatred. *Abhidharmadīpa* 192.
Theft, sexual misconduct with another's wife, and covetousness arise from greed;
false view arises from delusion; it is held that the others arise from all three.
The basis for each of these four should be known in their respective order:
sentient beings, then enjoyments, name-and-form, and name.
Taking life is the intentional killing of another without error.
Taking what is not given is said to be the appropriation of another's property that has not been relinquished.
Sexual misconduct consists of intentionally approaching the wife of another;
false speech is speaking otherwise than the truth with the intent to deceive one who understands the meaning. *Abhidharmadīpa* 196.
That which is apprehended by vision, hearing, and so forth, by the sense faculties, and by the mind, is respectively called the seen, the heard, the thought, and the known. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 197)
Slander is speech that causes division; harshness is that which is unpleasant; and frivolous chatter is afflicted speech, according to others, such as songs and the like. (Abhidharmadīpa 198)
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the longing for the property of others; ill-will (*vyāpāda*) has sentient beings as its object;
and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the view of non-causality arising from hatred. (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.78)
Volition is not itself the path of action; rather, it is by means of it that existence proceeds, even simultaneously with as many as eight unwholesome volitions.
By means of the ten wholesome [actions], up to five together with one and a half, [one attains higher realms];
whereas idle chatter, malice, and harsh speech ripen in hell in two ways.
In that same way, covetousness and false view are likewise considered [non-existent];
thus, the triad beginning with covetousness is absent there, as is idle chatter, which is of two kinds.
The ten unwholesome [faculties] are acquired elsewhere; the three wholesome ones are acquired everywhere.
Furthermore, for those in the formless realm, the noble ones, and those without perception, the seven material [faculties] are acquired through possession.
Excluding the Kurus and the hell-beings, they exist everywhere else in two ways;
all ten [paths of action] yield the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda*), and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Suffering arises from the infliction of pain; a short lifespan from killing;
and a lack of vigor from the destruction of vitality—this is its threefold fruit.
Karma on the path of immediate retribution possesses five fruits; however, noble karma that is stainless possesses four. Likewise, other wholesome or unwholesome karma [possesses four].
Other than that, the pure [result] is to be known; likewise, there are three neutral [results].
Of a wholesome [action], there are four, two, and three results, starting with the wholesome and so forth.
For an unwholesome [action], wholesome and other [minds] are respectively two, three, and four;
for an indeterminate [action], those same [minds], beginning with the wholesome, are respectively two, three, and three.
All four [kinds of karma] pertain to the past;
two pertain to the intermediate [present] existence; three pertain to one's own future birth; and two pertain to future births other than one's own.
Four [fruits] belong to one stage, or two or three belong to other stages;
for one in training (śaikṣa), there are three starting with that of training, and those same [three] belong to the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
One, three, and two [fruits] belong respectively to those beginning with the learner (śaikṣa) regarding the last [type of action];
however, for action to be abandoned by seeing (dṛgheya), there are two, two, and five [fruits] respectively.
Three, four, and one are taught as being abandoned by vision and so forth;
however, for that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, two, four, and three are considered to be of three kinds [respectively].
In sequence, one, two, or four [births] are for that karma which is not to be abandoned;
by one birth it is projected, and by many it is fulfilled.
Whether wholesome or unwholesome, whatever past action of one's own body, speech, or mind yields its fruit— that is considered "karmasvakatā" (the state of being the owner of one's own karma).
Conventionally, because the fruit of those actions is seen within the continuum of the aggregates, agency and enjoyership are taught; however, these are denied for that which is eternal.
There is a fourfold permutation regarding whether one possesses ownership of karma (karmasvakatā) and whether that [karma] exists:
the first case applies to one who abides in the fruit [of the path], because of the abandonment of that karma.
The second [type of person] is one who abides in the fruit of that [path], because of being connected with that karma;
the third is one endowed with both; but the fourth is one who possesses neither.
There may be ownership of karma, yet one will not experience its fruit;
this should be understood as occurring at the initial stage for one established in that fruit, up until the final fruit.
The second [type of karma] is that which has certain ripening (*dhruvapāka*), because its ripening is not subject to change;
the third is that which possesses both [certainty and intensity]; but the fourth is devoid of both.
There may be one who is possessed of karma yet does not experience its fruit;
this occurs in the case of past karma whose maturation has already been given, or in the case of future karma and so forth, which have not yet arisen. (Abhidharmadīpa 220)
The second [type of person] is one who possesses karma with certain ripening that has not yet been abandoned;
the third is one who is free from both; and the fourth is one who is devoid of both.
Some wise scholars say that unwholesome action is that which is performed improperly, defiled by the primary and secondary afflictions, and devoid of the characteristics of training and so forth.
From what point until when is a bodhisattva irreversible?
It is from the moment they don the armor of awakening, having committed themselves to the welfare of the world.
When one who does not go to the states of misery performs characteristic karma,
he is born into a great family with complete faculties and is devoted to gathering his own retinue.
Then, as a man endowed with the memory of past lives, eloquent, and possessed of wisdom, vigor, and action,
he attains manifestation among gods and humans.
For over three incalculable eons, he accumulates the ocean of qualities of the Dharma-body;
however, it is during the hundredth eon that he gathers the body which serves as its support.
Endowed with the thirty-two marks and radiant with the eighty secondary characteristics,
even the minds of enemies instantly become serene upon seeing him.
Mount Meru is destroyed by the wind at the end of an eon, the ocean by fire, and the thunderbolt by the thunderbolt; yet that mind remains unchanging.
That which belongs to the desire realm and is born of the sixth [consciousness] is of three kinds: compassion, faith, and the succession of others.
When a Buddha appears, a man or a woman attains that first thought.
To speak everything, to everyone, and at all times, while fulfilling the perfection of generosity;
and not abandoning self-restraint even unto death—this is called the excellence of ethical discipline (*śīla*).
Through the praise of Tiṣya, the perfection of vigor is attained; through the diamond-like [samādhi], that of wisdom;
and the fulfillment of all [perfections] is established in the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna).
The three bases of meritorious action and so forth are the teachings on the means for attaining that [Buddhahood];
likewise, the four foundations and the teaching of the seven true dharmas [are included therein].
The seven yogas, the three aggregates, and the three trainings and so forth have been taught;
likewise, the four perfections have also been proclaimed in the Vinaya.

The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening have been explicitly taught by the Self-Existent One as the causes for all forms of awakening, categorized as threefold according to their degrees of weakness and so forth.
Therefore, there is no path to awakening other than the three baskets (piṭaka) beginning with the Sūtras;
whoever here should speak of something other than this would be speaking the words of Māra.
This triad of great *asaṃkhyeya* eons is considered to be a distinct category called "the incalculable" (*asaṃkhya*), which stands above ordinary calculation.
The appearance of a Jina occurs during the period of decline, as long as the lifespan is one hundred years;
Pratyekabuddhas appear during both [phases], while Cakravartins appear only during the period of increase.
Their appearance is not held to occur below [a lifespan of] eighty thousand years;
by the power of their merit, they possess wheels made of gold, silver, copper, and iron.
Even when the means of accomplishment are equal, there is a distinction between them due to the difference in the sense faculties and so forth,
just as there is a difference in the results of giving between two mothers who both seek worldly existence and liberation.
Through the intensity of the cultivation of compassion, as well as through one's own self-awareness and mind,
the specific excellence of the Guru— who possesses the awareness of others— is likewise established.
The greatness of the Teacher is threefold, arising from his cause, his reality, and the emergence of his fruit;
for although liberation is equal for all three, they attain enlightenment.
When the Buddha is present before one, his Buddha-body is manifested;
each individual mark of the Sage is produced from a hundred such merits.
Just as the paths of action are [defined], so too are the three types of merit and so forth intended;
for generosity is that by which one gives, with regard to the welfare of oneself, others, and so on.

The karma of body and so forth is that very reality; furthermore, in some cases, it is called "non-informative" (avijñapti) by the Sage because of its predominance, for that indeed has great enjoyment as its fruit.
Some give gifts for the sake of accomplishing their own welfare and that of others;
others do so for the sake of following a virtuous course of conduct, and still others do so for neither purpose.
The excellence of the fruit is said to arise from the distinction of the giver, the object, and so forth;
thus, through qualities such as faith, the giver gives with acts of respect and the like.
From that [gift], one obtains a fruit endowed with qualities such as being honored;
an object perfected by color and other attributes bestows fruits such as physical beauty.
The field is distinguished by the factors known as virtue, suffering, and benefit;
and the mildness and so forth of the action [are determined] by the mildness and so forth of the intention and other such factors.
Giving to one who bestows the Dharma, to a child, to a father, to a mother, to a sick person,
to a Bodhisattva, and to one in a future existence is immeasurable.

The gift that a bodhisattva gives, as well as the eighth [type of gift] given by anyone else—that which is given by one who is wise to another who is worthy—is declared by the learned to be the most excellent. *Abhidharmadīpa* 250.
That which has been deliberated upon, projected, reinforced by fulfillment and so forth,
and from which the counteractive factors have departed— that is considered accumulated karma.
In acts such as worshipping a shrine, there arises a fruit even without a recipient, due to the mental factors consisting of the quality of renunciation toward one's own [possessions],
just like dwelling in loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
The nature of the gift of Dharma has as its object speech, reality, names, and so forth;
because its nature is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is not like the gift of food and other such things, which consist of names and so forth.
Ethical discipline (*śīla*) has been explained as form (*rūpa*) consisting of the beautiful (*śubha*), according to its various classifications;
however, in the treatise (*śāstra*), it is taught [as such] because it is predominant for the sake of rebirth in heaven (*svarga*).
That which is not defiled by faults such as immorality and the roots of unwholesomeness,
and which possesses the factors for the pacification of their opposites— that is what is called "pure" (śuddha) here.
But here, merit is concentrated; because it is the cultivation of the mind, it is preeminent for liberation, and thus it was taught by the All-Seeing One.
In this teaching, the roots of merit are briefly held to be of three kinds: those conducive to merit, those conducive to nirvāṇa, and likewise those conducive to penetration.
Writing, seals, and calculation are characterized by the actions of body and speech;
furthermore, numbering should be understood as having the nature of mental action.
Since the world, under their influence, is inclined toward what should not be done and partakes in suffering,
I shall explain those afflictions— the bonds of existence such as attachment and the rest.

However, those [factors] such as the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are designated by names derived from the specific qualities arising from their own inherent capacities, having assumed general designations.
Attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, doubt, and wrong views—
these six are declared to be the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that obstruct the gateway to the higher good.
Due to the twofold division of attachment, seven are considered; due to the divisions of views, ten are recorded.
Furthermore, ninety-eight should be known through the distinctions of realms, aspects, and so forth.
Attachment is divided into two types: attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and that which is called attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*).
This distinction arises primarily from the difference between outward engagement and inward dwelling.
The view of a self-identity, the two types of grasping at extremes, false view,
as well as the esteeming of views and the esteeming of precepts and observances— these are the five views.
In this context, ten [defilements] are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering; seven are destroyed by the vision of the cause;
seven are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation; and eight are destroyed by the vision of the path.
Because they take as their objects what is to be abandoned by vision and because they grasp at the aspects of existence,
the four [afflictions] beginning with attachment are to be known as exhausted by both paths.
Because they arise by the power of each respective kalpa, views and doubt [are abandoned] upon the destruction of vision;
it is the same for form, and likewise for the formless, except for the latent tendency of resistance.
Those [defilements] at the peak of existence (bhavāgra) that are to be abandoned by patience (kṣānti) are considered to be abandoned only by insight (dṛg).
However, those which are to be destroyed by knowledge (jñāna) in that [peak of existence], their destruction occurs only through cultivation (abhyāsa).
The view that "I" and "mine" is known as the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi);
the two graspings at annihilation and permanence are considered the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
The denial of cause and effect is called wrong view;
the grasping at inferior things as supreme is to be known as the adherence to views.
Indeed, that which is called "asceticism and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) pertains to what is causeless and the wrong path;
because it is the grasping of a wrong path through delusion regarding suffering, it is to be discarded by [the correct] view.
Because the severance of the view of a self-identity arises from the observation of mere phenomena,
and because that occurs during the clear realization of suffering, it is therefore to be abandoned by the vision of that [truth] alone.
Two [of the perversions] arise from the adherence to views, one from the view of a self-identity, and the other half from the grasping at extremes; thus are the perversions conceptualized.
Because they function through investigation, superimposition, and error,
the term "perversion" (viparyāsa) applies to these very [factors] by virtue of their nature as views, mind, and perception.
There are seven types of conceit based on the three [realms], and nine types of conceit categorized in three ways;
these threefold divisions arise from such things as excessive inflation, and from the notions of "I am superior" and so forth, as well as from existence and non-existence.
The outbursts of violence and the like, remorse, and unwholesome views,
as well as the desire for non-existence, do not arise in a noble one due to the absence of their causes.
The establishment of all [afflictions] belonging to the universal category occurs through suffering and its origin;
this applies to all those types that are to be abandoned by the vision of those two truths.
Doubt, the five views, ignorance—whether mixed with those [views] or independent—these seven are universal. From among these, four arise from the [truth of] suffering.
Substantially, there are eleven; by name, they are considered to be seven.
However, attachment, aversion, and pride function as determinative [factors].
Because they exist in different modes, they all-pervade their own respective realms at once;
because they take other realms as their objects, those previously mentioned are indeed all-pervading.

Among those [defilements], nine belong to the higher realms; of these, the first two are excluded from the two views. Their co-existent factors, with the exception of their acquisitions, are also omnipresent.

Furthermore, ignorance associated with doubt and false view, as well as ignorance alone—these six are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path; they do not exist for one who possesses pure vision.
Nirvāṇa belongs only to its own level, while one established on the path belongs to nine levels;
their respective objects of perception are mutually related through the state of being causes by way of causal efficacy.
There is no passion because it lacks a causal basis; no hatred because there is no offense;
no pride because of extreme tranquility; and no other views because of the nature of vision.
A universal latent disposition (anuśaya) adheres to its entire [sphere], belonging to its own element;
a non-universal one, however, adheres to its own level by way of its object and to its own category.
Because it is not accepted [as an object] and because it is an adverse state, it does not have the higher stages or the Path as its sphere;
however, it exists through association with its own associated factors when they are not abandoned.
Because these adhere [to the person] through the logic of the nurse’s garment and the stain, and by way of the movements of birds and aquatic creatures,
they are therefore known as *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
Because these [defilements] adhere even to the moments of atoms through their modes such as self-love (*svairiṣṭa*) and so forth,
they are therefore considered *anuśaya*s (latent dispositions).
The first two views are considered obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the desire realm;
however, in the two [higher] realms, all defilements (*mala*) are likewise obscured-unspecified.
The remaining [defilements] are unwholesome regarding sensual pleasures; therefore, greed, hatred, and delusion are the three roots of the unwholesome by virtue of their connection with five reasons.
The three roots corresponding to the two neutral [roots] are ignorance, intellect, and craving; they are not doubt, pride, or views. (Abhidharmadīpa 291)
Because it is mobile, because it exists above, and because it is non-pervasive— respectively,
due to a failure to understand the meaning of the Sūtra, [the argument] is not a valid reason, since it is an exhortation addressed to a meditator.
The best of speakers explained the four ways of answering questions and the fourfold set of positions for the sake of training his disciples in debate.
There are four types of [answers]: that which is categorical, that which is analytical, that which is by way of questioning, and that which is to be set aside;
as in the cases of death, birth, excellence, life, and the difference between substances.
One is designated as "speaking of the basis" (sthānavāditva), another is called "conceptual construction" (parikalpa);
another is named "the path" (pratipad), and another is designated as "speaking of knowledge" (jñānavāditva).
One who exists with pride, aversion, and attachment that have not abandoned their activity is bound to that object in which they have arisen and are not yet abandoned.

The continuum of the aggregates (skandhasantati) is associated everywhere with these unarisen mental [factors], with all others belonging to its own time-period, and likewise with all remaining factors that have not yet arisen.
In this context, only two [of the three natures] are established as real, while the third exists only figuratively;
for it is the cause of both existence and non-existence, and because it is embraced by those who stand in the middle.
"All exists," "there is a partial existence," "all does not exist," and another,
"the proponent of the indeterminate existence"— these are remembered as the four proponents.
Among these, the first proponent possesses correctness;
however, the others are merely conceited in their logic, being excluded from both reasoning and scripture.
Because he maintains the existence of the three time periods and the three constants by virtue of their functional efficacy, the first [school] is called Sarvāstivāda; it is of four types.

There are two known as the "change-of-state" (bhāvānyathika) and the "change-of-characteristic" (lakṣaṇānyathika); another is the "change-of-condition" (avasthānyathika); and yet another is the "change-of-otherness" (anyathānyathika), which is the third, belonging to the proponents of logic.
He maintains that the distinction between the time periods is established by way of activity (*kāritra*):
while performing that activity, it is the present period; once the activity has been performed, it is the past; and when the activity has not yet been performed, it is the other (the future).
That sign which is perceived by the intellect is to be known as fourfold:
in terms of ultimate reality, in terms of conventional reality, in terms of both, and also in terms of relative dependence.
The past and the unarisen exist, because the Buddha taught them as being like the present;
and because they are not objects of cognition, their existence is like that of the present.
Based on scripture and reasoning, cognition does not have a non-existent object as its support;
furthermore, the negation of a relationship between a horse and a horn occurs only in dependence upon something else.
When a real entity such as form has perished, a cognition nevertheless arises;
that cognition has the aspect of non-existence for knowledge, just like the mind of the Teacher or other minds.
Because it serves as the basis for the arising of joy, fear, agitation, and the production of mindfulness,
the capacity of the whole [cognition] is manifested, like the form of a jar together with its lamp.
Because it is to be accomplished by the agent of the act of procreation (*janīhā*), like the five transformations of being (*bhāvavikāra*);
and because its status as a factor of action is seen in that which exists, like objects that are to be modified (*vikārya*) or reached (*prāpya*).
A second birth of an entity that has already been born is not possible;
since primary existence is absent due to the lack of qualities, secondary existence does not exist.
When there is a similarity of properties, the usage [of a term] for that which possesses it is like sweet speech;
the birth of the primary [meaning], which is possessed of gender, is like a son and so forth.
The sky might be filled with sky-flowers, and a frog might possess matted hair,
if intrinsic nature were to arise having previously been non-existent through the power of mental cultivation.

O gentle one, tell me: how can a thing attain the status of a real entity through dependent origination, when its phenomena have abandoned the power of stability and are accompanied by destruction and arising? Abhidh-d_313
In the world, mutual benefit is observed only between two existing things;
likewise, mutual injury is also not observed between a horse's horn and a snake's feet.
Whatever is dependently originated does not exist by way of intrinsic nature;
that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature exists in a manner other than that.

Causes merely bring about the state [of manifestation] for an entity that already exists, just as ministers bring about the kingship of a prince who already possesses the nature of a king. (Abhidharmadīpa 316)
When there is a collection of dharmas, their efficacy arises,
just as that of accumulated atoms for the perception of a self.
For one for whom past karma is non-existent and future fruit is non-existent,
it is evident that a son of a barren woman is born from an intermediate state being.
Because it lacks the characteristics of a real entity and because its status as a substantial reality is not established,
the future and the past do not possess the nature of conceptual reality (*prajñaptisatya*).
What is the obstacle? It is the deficiency of the limbs; that [deficiency] does not exist at all times for everyone.
Therefore, listen to this from the virtuous: the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is indeed difficult to understand. Abhidh-d_320.

The projection of a fruit by that which has acquired its capacity through its arrival at the present time-path and through the acquisition of its constituent parts of the causal complex is designated as "activity" (kāritra).
The nature of form is neither its present state nor its past or unborn states;
therefore, it is not maintained that the essence of form undergoes alteration through its movement through the time-periods (adhvan).
A certain state arises for an existing entity;
likewise there is power, likewise time, likewise existence, and likewise activity.
The world is pervaded by conceptual constructions that delight the minds of fools;
however, those conceptual constructions that capture the minds of the wise are difficult to find.
One who is bound by other universal [defilements] remains so even when the vision of suffering has been abandoned;
likewise, even when a previous category has been abandoned, one remains bound by the remaining [defilements] that take those [abandoned categories] as their object.
Sixteen dharmas are to be known, each consisting of the three realms of existence;
likewise, there are five kinds of pure [dharmas] and the same number of consciousnesses.
One should observe the elements, the sense bases, the truths, and their various modes,
impelled by the latent dispositions of the knowledge that discerns and the knowledge that comprehends phenomena.

Those [factors] belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, are the objects of the mind; they consist of three of their own [realms], one of the form realm, and the stainless [unconditioned].
Those born of the form realm have as their objects the three lower [realms] belonging to themselves, one higher [realm], and the pure;
those pertaining to the formless realm have as their objects those belonging to the three realms, the threefold [objects], and the pure.
All [these] have more to be known than themselves; they possess equal departure, vision, and destruction [of defilements];
they are free from afflictions, have attained the three realms of existence, and have as their final object of focus the stainless [state].
That which belongs to the realm of desire has the five objects as its sphere; that which belongs to the realm of form has eight objects as its range;
that which belongs to the formless realm pertains to ten [consciousnesses], while the stainless [uncontaminated] pertains to ten alone.
In the consciousness that has objects belonging to the higher realms and the sense-pleasures (kāma),
the three [types of] universal proclivities (anuśaya) belonging to their own level and those of the form realm (rūpa) which are to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) lie latent.
Four [types of abandonment] belong to one's own sphere; furthermore, three belonging to the realm of form, along with all those belonging to the formless realm, are abandoned through cultivation.

In exactly the same way, they also increase in relation to the second [category], likewise in the fifth, and in the third as well; those with outflows (sāsrava) increase in relation to their own [category].
But when [the mind] has turned away [from the desire realm], those [knowledges] pertaining to the desire realm have conditioned objects as their support;
the remainder is to be explained as before, and in the fourth [dhyāna] it is like the third.
But when [the path] has been transformed, the four [factors] belonging to the desire realm are as before;
in the first [dhyāna] of the form realm, there are three below, and indeed three in its own [level].
The formless [attainments] are all-pervading, together with those abandoned through the path of cultivation;
when there is a transition [of rebirth], three arise from below and four from their own realm.
The four categories belonging to the formless realm also increase [as latent dispositions];
likewise in the second [dhyāna], and similarly in the fifth as well.
Those [defilements] which have the contaminated as their object, as well as those belonging to their own level, also increase in the third;
however, when there is a transformation, those pertaining to the form realm increase in relation to the objects of conditioned phenomena.
The rest, however, should be understood as before; in the fourth [dhyāna] it is like the third.
One should understand that when there is a revolution [of the basis] like that of the third, it occurs in the first formless realm (ārūpya).
Three [types of faculties] belong to the desire realm; three belong to the form realm;
and likewise for the third and fifth [turnings], they are as in the case of the form realm when there is a transformation.

Furthermore, in the third [transformation], when one's own [basis] has undergone revolution, those [consciousnesses] which formerly had as their objects the contaminated things belonging to one's own realm now have as their objects the conditioned things belonging to one's own realm.
Up to the point where they are called "otherness" and so forth, it should be explained in the fourth [case] just as in the third;
however, when consciousness has undergone transformation, the wise one should designate it just as in the first.

The category [of defilements] to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, along with all the omnipresent [defilements], lies latent in two realms; those belonging to the formless realm lie latent in the eye-faculty.
The aggregates belonging to the realms of desire and form, which fall within the range of the visual faculty, are of three types each:
those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, by the vision of its cause, and by cultivation.
The formless [defilements] are to be abandoned by cultivation and all-pervading; they persist as latent tendencies.
However, when there is a transformation [of the basis], four [remain], excluding those associated with equanimity and those to be abandoned by insight.
Regarding the faculty of suffering, however, that which belongs to the desire realm [is associated] with its own [mental factors] along with the universal ones;
but as for the consciousness within its sphere, the categories of latent dispositions (anuśaya) adhere to it.
The three [types of] form that have entered the realm of desire are abandoned through universal cultivation;
however, when there is a transition to another [realm], the four [types] belonging to the realm of desire continue to underlie as latent dispositions.

From the final existence in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), all universal [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) and four others adhere [to the mind] due to the non-transformation of the two [opposites]. (Abhidharmadīpa 349)
In the faculty of pleasure, in the mind that takes it as its object, and also in the sphere of its activity,
the proclivities belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as the universal ones, lie dormant according to their respective conditions.

However, all [factors] comprised within the three realms are included in the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the consciousness that takes it as its object; they have all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) as their sphere of activity.
Only those [defilements] that have conditioned phenomena as their object persist in the transformation;
there is no distinction whatsoever here regarding the twofold transformation.

From a mind that is to be abandoned by seeing suffering and so forth, six minds arise immediately thereafter for one who possesses desire; from such a mind in the higher realms, five or five [minds] arise.
One should specify the minds of one born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) as being either one, five, six, seven, or ten. *Abhidharmadīpa* 354.
One should characterize these minds of one born in the formless realm as being fivefold belonging to their own realm at the time of death, and tenfold from elsewhere.
Because it acts as an associate and because it lies latent within, the mind is considered "with proclivities" (sānuśaya);
it is designated as being of two kinds—defiled and non-defiled—or in one way [as being with proclivities].

From delusion arises the view of a self-identity; from that, the view of grasping at extremes; from that, doubt and false views; and from those, the esteeming of morality and ascetic practices, and then the esteeming of [wrong] views.
Attachment and pride extend toward one's own [view], while hatred extends toward others;
this sequence of theirs should be understood as such due to the predominance of their respective functions.
However, due to association with good or bad friends, the lack of restraint in their conduct is considered [the cause];
some affliction arises when all three causes are complete. (Abhidharmadīpa 359)
All afflictions (kleśa) accompanied by ignorance (avidyā) in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) are considered the outflow of desire (kāmāsrava).
Excluding sloth (styāna) and restlessness (auddhatya), those [afflictions] in the higher realms are the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava), because they are similar [in nature].
But that which is called ignorance is the root; therefore, it is ignorance throughout all realms.
Likewise, the floods and yokes exclude [wrong] views; their separate enumeration, however, is due to their intensity.
That ignorance constitutes two types of clinging as previously described, while the two consisting of views constitute another;
all four together form one [type of clinging], because they rely upon wrong paths and so forth.

The remaining [defilements] belong to the three realms; however, in the final [category], they are presented in five ways through terms such as "fetters" (saṃyojana) and so forth, according to their manifestation within the personal existence (sātmabhāva).
In this [system], there are nine fetters (saṃyojana), including envy and avarice;
because of their commonality as objects and their lack of endurance, views constitute two fetters.
The remaining five latent dispositions (anuśaya) are further divided fivefold each;
they are taught as those conducive to the lower realm (avarabhāgīya) and those conducive to the higher realm (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
The first and last two views, as well as doubt and sensual desire, each occur twice;
by two [factors] there is no transcendence of desires, and by three there is a return to them.
Because it is stated that two and one are to be abandoned by vision, and because they are grasped by way of what is to be abandoned by vision,
these three are thus exemplified, even though they all share the quality of being abandonable by vision.
Because they are the source of all misfortune, because they act as adversaries to the Path,
and because they lack correct reasoning, the three fetters (saṃyojana) are taught.
Two are the attachments born of the realms of form and formlessness; three arise from pride and delusion.
Because they underlie the three types of sensation and because of their firmness, they constitute the three bonds.
Because they are composed in two sections each, four treatises are proclaimed:
those titled *Abhidhyā* (Covetousness), as well as *Dveṣa* (Hatred) and the two *Parāmarśas* (Graspings).
The secondary afflictions (upakleśa), such as impetuosity (saṃrambha) and the rest, should be understood as they have been described;
or alternatively, all afflicted mental factors designated as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are to be known as such.
The other root afflictions and impurities are designated as the six secondary afflictions:
dissimulation, enmity, spite, deceit, intoxication, and harmfulness.
Envy, jealousy, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, sloth, torpor, restlessness, anger, avarice, and remorse— these are the ten types of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
From these [afflictions], shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and so forth are the outflows of attachment (*anunaya*);
concealment (*mrakṣa*), lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), torpor (*styāna*), drowsiness (*middha*), and so forth arise from delusion (*moha*).
Regret arises from doubt; anger and the like originate from hatred;
while negligence, arrogance, malice, deceit, guile, and dissimulation arise from delusion.
Coarseness of body and so forth should be known as arising from a mixture [of afflictions];
malice is the outflow of the adherence to views, and deceit is the outflow of views.
It is taught that attachment is associated with mental pleasure and physical pleasure,
while aversion is associated with mental displeasure and physical pain.
Delusion is associated with all [mental factors]; false view with two mental factors;
doubt with dissatisfaction; and for the remaining [afflictions], with mental joy.
However, this rule applies to all [factors] belonging to the desire realm by way of equanimity;
but for those born from other realms, [the abandonment occurs] through their own [factors] corresponding to each respective level.
From envy, from dejection, from remorse, and likewise from anger, from malice and resentment, and similarly from harmfulness.
Avarice [is associated] with mental distress; for some, it is with mental ease.
Likewise, deceit, guile, concealment, and torpor are associated with both. (Abhidharmadīpa 381)
Pride is associated with the aggregate of mental formations and with pleasure;
lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, and restlessness are associated with all five [faculties].
Lack of shame, lack of dread, lethargy, torpor, and likewise restlessness.
By means of the final [knowledge], which takes all [objects] as its support, one understands those [defilements] through their impermanence and other characteristics;
or, by means of the final [knowledge] with mixed objects, there is the absolute destruction of the defilements.
These three have as their object a meaning that is undifferentiated; they are held to be twofold.
