For one who sees in this way, there is the direct perception of arising and passing away.
It subsequently arises within the aggregates like the whirling of a firebrand;
he thus contemplates the dependent origination of the aggregates.
Having caused him to fall upon the [Four] Truths, someone then examines him;
having fully realized their impermanence and suffering, he does so once again.
Seeing that [all things] are without an agent, devoid of activity, and arise dependent upon conditions, one cultivates the aspect of reality: "there is no self" in all of them.
For one who perceives both the lack of a presiding controller and dependence in all phenomena,
a firm intellect regarding selflessness proceeds.
Because it is not empty of intrinsic nature, it is declared to be the Seal of the Dharma;
and because it is stated as such, the aspect of emptiness is not taught.

One should constantly examine the lineages, doors, aggregates, and so forth, as well as the elements and other categories, according to their respective specific and general characteristics. *Abhidharmadīpa* 391.
Then, for each aggregate (skandha), through its intrinsic nature and so forth,
skill regarding the seven points of stability subsequently arises in him in due order according to reality.
For him who, accompanied by faith and vigor, seeks the fire of the knowledge of reality, there arises, through gradual friction, the fire-drill of the existence of the truth of suffering.
From that, there arises knowledge conforming to the aspects, which leads to the determination of tranquility; it consists of cultivation, is called "Heat," and is accompanied by its followers.
Then, in the same way, the Summits (mūrdhan) destroy false views;
because they possess greater power than the Heat-stages (ūṣman), they further increase faith in the Jewels.
...and in both of these cases, the latter [alternative] is the correct one.
The view of a self in the aggregates and so forth is not cultivated by one who perceives nirvāṇa;
however, one should point out that the mental aspects (ākāra) are of the same kind everywhere in this context.
One of those [four] is to be seen as present during the stage of increase;
however, one of the other four is present during the stage of increase.
In this case, all four [foundations of mindfulness] are certainly cultivated in their future state;
indeed, when liberation is imminent, they all exist in their entirety as future states.
Indeed, all aspects are cultivated through the acquisition of the lineage;
however, upon the acquisition of the lineage, it should be understood that there is cultivation of the concordant aspects.
In the case of the "all-pervading" [attainment], at the peak [of the path], and during the intensification through the non-manifestation of cessation,
the four called "Dharma" are indeed present and future.
Therein, all aspects are cultivated through the acquisition of the lineage;
having arisen from any one of all [the truths], they increase during the cultivation of the three truths.
In that [state], four future [moments] are cultivated with certainty;
all aspects (ākāra) should be known [to be cultivated]. Listen regarding their application during the stage of Receptivity (kṣānti).
In all cases, the four final [knowledges] have arisen, while indeed four future ones exist;
therein, all aspects are cultivated, and they too are future.
The application of mindfulness called "dharma" pertains to the present supreme dharmas;
however, all four are cultivated in relation to those [future ones], because of the certainty regarding them.

Indeed, there are four aspects because they resemble the path of seeing; this should be understood in the same way as with the heat [of the aids to penetration] on the path of seeing. *Abhidharmadīpa* 406.
One should indicate that at the final moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), the present [knowledge] is directed toward it;
likewise, there are four future [knowledges], which constitute the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Furthermore, even above that, when all previously unarisen qualities arise for the Noble One,
[the path] consists of hearing and reflection, having abandoned [the coarse] and having removed the most subtle of the subtle.
On the path of the beginner, through the conquest of the four stages,
one indeed attains four future knowledges from among those [eight] regarding the elements.
In the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), all [future] factors are acquired; in the final [moment], they are all future.
In the last dhyāna, within the eight paths beginning with the preparatory stage (*prayoga-mārga*), it is as previously stated.
One should know that there are three [factors] in the ninth [dhyāna] due to the entry into the fundamental stage;
however, in the preliminary application (*sāmantaka*), there are four, or else it may be the last one.
In the case of the supernormal powers of the divine eye and ear, as well as in the liberations and so forth,
one [knowledge] is present, while four are indeed future.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds, there are three [kinds of objects], while for the four immeasurables and the recollection of past lives, there are four; for the last [knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows], all [objects] are future.
Regarding the formless liberations (ārūpya-vimokṣas), one may speak of any one of the three;
however, when they have actually arisen before one's eyes, one should specify only those three.
However, regarding the final [attainment] of the formless and the totalities (kṛtsna), one should cite it as being present;
but when speaking of the three that have not yet arisen, one must certainly speak of them as such.
Indeed, for a noble one (ārya) in the application toward detachment, as well as in the process of casting it off, all [the factors] are present;
furthermore, four future ones have also arisen from among the others.
In the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*), all future [qualities] except for the last are liberated;
however, in the case of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth, one should point out that all qualities belong exclusively to the non-noble (*anārya*).
And regarding the final [birth], former abodes, and so forth, as well as the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharmapratisaṃvid),
likewise regarding the obstruction to the undertaking of other meditative concentrations, and in that same way.
Likewise, when subtle perception arises in the formless liberations and so forth,
four future [dharmas] that have not yet become any of the others indeed exist.
But regarding the most subtle [object], one should say that there is one past [moment] and three future ones;
this cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness has thus been explained in brief.
This aid to penetration is fourfold, consists of cultivation, belongs to six stages, and has sixteen aspects; it comprises the five aggregates, excluding acquisitions.
But subsequently, there is indeed penetration called the Noble Path;
because it is a certain penetration, it is therefore termed "penetration" (nirvedha).
In regard to suffering, there is a delight in the knowledge of the dharma, which is the stainless vision of the dharma;
immediately thereafter, there is a firm resolve toward that very same [suffering], which is the subsequent knowledge of the dharma.
In this way, for each of the three truths, there are likewise two types of subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*).
Among these, the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) should be known as consisting of fifteen moments, as they do not extend beyond that point.
The final moment [of the path] is the path of cultivation; this is the fruit, by virtue of the accomplishment of the goal.
The fifth [type of noble person] proceeds to the Akaniṣṭha heaven by means of the intermingling of the dhyānas;
another goes to the formless realm in four ways; and yet another attains nirvāṇa in this very life.
Furthermore, having divided each of these three into three again, there are nine [types] belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Their specific distinctions should be understood through the differentiation of karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).
The six [types of beings] together with those who flow upwards constitute the sevenfold "good destination" (sadgati).
Because their activity does not lead to liberation, it is said that only these [six] possess a good destination.
For the Noble One whose existence has been transformed does not go to another realm here;
he is one who proceeds upward and is incapable of falling away from his attainment.
The final [moment] is desired first because of the mixing of the two moments for the sake of emergence,
for the sake of bliss, and indeed for the sake of apprehending the afflictions.
Due to its fivefold nature, it is known as the five Pure Abodes;
they have never before been seen by any ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
He who attains the attainment of cessation is a body-witness;
he is one who has abandoned eight parts of the peak of existence and is a candidate for arhatship.

And for one who abides in the final path of immediate succession called "diamond-like," is the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) directed toward that fruit, having it as its single object, or not? Abhidh-d_433 //
Upon attaining that, he becomes one beyond training (aśaikṣa), an Arhat honored by the three worlds,
dissociated from all afflictions, and one who has reached the further shore of the threefold training.
The path called cultivation is twofold, distinguished by being either with outflows or without outflows;
however, that called seeing should be understood as entirely without outflows.
It should be understood that for those who have gradually attained detachment to a greater or lesser degree,
as well as for those who are not yet detached, that which is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) is likewise eternally stainless.
The stainless one transcends the peak of existence.
Because, having abandoned that which is with distinction, one attains the supreme fruit:
for the learner (śaikṣa), by means of three [faculties] beginning with the faculty of non-decline; for the perfected one (arhat), by means of two.
Furthermore, the path should be understood, in brief, as being fourfold:
that which is called the uninterrupted [path] and the path of liberation, characterized by the commencement and the excellence [of the fruit].
For one of sharp faculties, the path is easy in the fundamental dhyānas;
for one of dull intellect, it is slow elsewhere due to the opposite conditions.
Enlightenment (bodhi) is considered to be the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) as well as the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādadhī);
its factors consist of eleven [dharmas], which are thirty-seven by name.
It consists of equanimity, joy, and volition, along with the five faculties beginning with faith;
it arises from two aspects together with pliancy, though there is a difference in its names according to perspective.
In this context, the powers are the faculties themselves; wisdom is the application of mindfulness;
energy is called the right efforts; and the bases of psychic power are the stabilization of the mind.
That which simultaneously effects the abandonment of faults, the non-arising [of further faults], the production of virtues, and their increase—
that indeed is the fourfold abandonment.
The bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) are the concentrations drawn forth by desire, exertion, investigation, and the mind;
they are the four sources for the perfection of qualities.
The five faculties, beginning with faith, are called "faculties" because they exercise mastery over the three types of enlightenment;
that same group is described by the term "powers" because they are not overcome.
The seven factors of enlightenment were taught by the Teacher for the purpose of awakening;
they are called "enlightenment" in the ultimate sense because they provide assistance up to the very end through wisdom.
Due to the reasons already stated, joy, tranquility, and equanimity are considered factors [of the dhyānas];
the four beginning with intention are to be understood as such because they are conducive to the Path.
This path has the light of knowledge, the ground of subtle conceptualization, virtue as its retinue, and mindfulness and vigor as its friends;
it enjoys the supreme bliss of all meditative concentrations and reaches the abode of the two kinds of liberation.
The predominance of the sevenfold group should be understood, respectively, in the stages of "heat" and so forth, as well as in the paths of cultivation and vision.
The mind is not [itself] "volition" because it is like a king; because it follows after qualities and defects;
and because it conforms to conventional usage—therefore, these [terms] are not accepted as synonyms for it.
Because it is inclined toward the fruit of maturation and because the Path has been taught, it is not volition;
nor is it attention, due to its lack of predominance and because it sets in motion both knowledge and ignorance.
It is not *chanda* because it prioritizes the commencement of action; it is not *vīrya* because it does not augment vigor;
it is not *adhimokṣa* because of its superimposition; and it is not *sparśa* because it is difficult to discern.
In the noble lineage, there is no sense of shame or dread of blame because of a lack of proficiency in conduct;
there is no heedfulness because it is subordinate to others; and there is no non-harming because of the absence of malice.
Because they function by taking sentient beings as their basis, loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth are not [the faculties];
nor are the clear realizations (avetyaprasādas), because they are only a partial portion of the factors of the path and the faculties.
There is no aversion toward the roots of virtue because they are the sphere of sentient beings;
there is no [desire for] nirvāṇa due to indifference, nor is there [attachment to] the voices of others because of their remoteness.
The factors of enlightenment are free from passion because they are in the state closest to awakening;
other [factors] to be fully understood may be either with stain or without stain.

In the first dhyāna, all [hindrances] are eliminated; in the fundamental [dhyānas], they are removed by joy (*prīti*); in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), they are removed by both; in the second dhyāna, even discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) are eliminated; and in the two [higher dhyānas], they are removed by these two [joy and discursive thought] respectively.
They should be understood as being derived from the factors of morality (*śīlāṅga*) and from those two [the meditative concentrations] within the three formless realms;
and from all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), with the exception of the factors of enlightenment, within the desire realm.
Regarding those four which are first mentioned therein by the learned,
they occur during the stages of *nyāma*, the entry [into the path], detachment, the attainment of the fruit, and the increase of the faculties.

Regarding the eight path-factors free from passion (*nīrajaska*), their acquisition and non-acquisition across the various time-periods (*adhvan*) should be understood as residing in nine bases (*āśraya*), according to their respective cases. *Abhidharmadīpa* 461.
Upon the realization of the three truths, there is the acquisition of confidence in the ethical discipline and the Dharma;
and upon the vision of the truth of the path, there is also the acquisition of confidence in the Buddha and the Sangha as objects of focus.
The faith directed toward the Path and so forth, which has the Truths as its object, arising from the Buddhist Saṅgha and due to the power of present realization,
is this "verified clarity regarding the Dharma" (dharmāvetyaprasāda).

Faith in the qualities of that Buddha— who is himself awakened through the opening of the eye of wisdom by the destruction of the darkness of the sleep of delusion— is considered "serene confidence" (prasāda) toward the Victor.
Faith that has those qualities as its object—the source of persons enriched with the virtues of those in training and those beyond training—is clarity; it is the sphere of the Saṅkha.
The stainlessness of the precepts is indeed clarity (*prasāda*);
substantially these are two, but nominally they are four. *Abhidharmadīpa* 466.
Because the learner (śaikṣa) still possesses remaining bonds, liberation (vimukti) is not considered a limb [of the path].
It is twofold, being of the nature of conviction regarding liberation and consisting of either permanence or impermanence.
For that very awakening previously described is called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
The future mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is liberated from the obstruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
In the world, one who engages in the activity of the Dharma is considered to be engaged in what is righteous;
however, the Path, having taken up its functional activity, casts off that obscuration.
That very liberation which is eternal is what is designated as the three elements—dispassion and so forth—in the Sūtra; for the threefold division is made in consideration of different perspectives.
Dispassion (*virāga*) is the liberation from passion; that which is called abandonment (*prahāṇa*) is the destruction of other [defilements];
and the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*) is the cessation of other things characterized by grasping (*sopādāna*).
The yogin becomes weary through an intellect that takes suffering and its cause as its object;
however, one who is attached becomes detached from it—thus there are four alternatives.

The perceptions are the ten beginning with the perception of impermanence; from those [arise] the three beginning with the foul. The path is the method of the path; the last four are the path, and the final three are the fruit.
The three types of perceptions of impurity and so forth should be known as being with outflows (*sāsrava*); they are defiled.
However, the others are stainless; the nine stages of awakening (*bodhi*) are stainless.
One should observe the final [perfection] within the last eleven stages;
one should know that the fourth, fifth, and sixth [perfections] exist within the first seven stages.
This world, deluded regarding reality, is bewildered about the reality of what is to be known;
I shall explain those forms of knowledge in detail, beginning with their essential natures.
Having set aside [the categories of] genus and substance, its tenfold division is proclaimed by the names of dharma-knowledge and so forth, in consideration of its opposites and other factors.
There are two [knowledges] regarding the specific objects of dharma and subsequent [knowledge], four regarding suffering and so forth,
two regarding conventional [knowledge] and other-minds, and two regarding cessation and non-arising.
Its establishment should be understood through the application of antidotes, by way of intrinsic nature, aspect, and object, or by means of its function or accumulation.

In order to eliminate delusion regarding the elements (dhātu), the truths (satya), the objects (artha), and the mind (citta), as well as regarding birth, destruction, and non-arising, their classification is indeed tenfold.
The comprehension of thorough knowledge and so forth regarding suffering and the rest is the fruit of the cognition of destruction.
The steadfast one always performs what ought to be done; those with mental forms, however, are dependent on supports.
The knowledge of others' minds consists of three [knowledges]; the cognition of phenomena is one; the cognition of cessation is one;
these constitute the four foundations of mindfulness; any other [cognition] is considered a knowledge distinct from them.
The path, the dharma-knowledge, and the subsequent knowledge are the objects of the ninefold cognition.
Having divided the five dharmas— which pertain to the three realms, consist of the path, and are eternal—
into two types for the sake of exposition, one should demonstrate the sphere of knowledge.
In the first cognition of the path of seeing, one is endowed with three cognitions;
in each of the [subsequent] four, there is an increase by one; beyond that, one who is detached [from the realm] possesses another mind through wisdom.
In the detachment from the three dhyānas and the desire realm, in the final path to liberation,
and in the preparatory stage of the fundamental dhyānas, the cultivation of the future [dharmas] is to be known.
Likewise, in the case of an ordinary person (*bāla*) generating the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth,
as well as during the paths of preparation (*prayoga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), there is a conventional knowledge of other minds.
In the path of vision, the patiences and knowledges of their own respective types are cultivated;
likewise, conventional knowledge is cultivated during the subsequent knowledges concerning suffering and its cause.

Because they have a common counteragent and because one proceeds toward the path within them, it is therefore called "clear realization" (abhisamaya); this is due to the attainment of the end of those three truths.
In the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) termed "the path," six or seven [knowledges] are cultivated;
furthermore, in the uninterrupted path (ānantarya-mārga) and above, no other mental cognition is cultivated.
In the paths of abandonment and liberation, prior to the final liberation,
conventional knowledge is not cultivated because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).
That which extends without obstruction regarding the intrinsic nature and other aspects of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and so forth,
and is designated as the knowledge of the meditative absorptions and so forth— that is the power consisting of the nine knowledges.

That which operates in the discernment of the faculties of sentient beings, their dullness or sharpness, and so forth, is the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; it consists of nine types of cognition.
That which operates with respect to the threefold inclinations of sentient beings— beginning with the inferior—
and which is designated as the cognition of various inclinations, is the power consisting of nine types.
That which is called the consideration of various elements (nānādhātu) and proceeds for the sake of sentient beings,
consisting of nine types of knowledge— such is the power of the wisdom regarding various elements.

That knowledge which understands the distinctions among destinies, dharmas, and noble ones according to their various conditions—that wisdom constitutes the power of the path leading everywhere. *Abhidharmadīpa* 497.
That which is called conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) perceiving one's own past births is considered the power of recollecting former lives (pūrvajātyanusmṛtijñānabala), together with its fruit.
The knowledge regarding the passing away and rebirth of sentient beings that functions across other time periods is called the power of the cognition of death and rebirth; it is described as before.
The cognition of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) is designated as such; it consists of six cognitions, or alternatively, ten.
Here, the first [cognition] has sixteen aspects, while the others have more, according to their respective stages.
The seventh has sixteen aspects and two undivided forms;
the second, however, has eight aspects and consists of nine knowledges.
The power of the Tathāgata is said to be known in twelve forms:
the first has all things as its object, while the last relies upon tranquility.
The seventh [knowledge] has two types of objects: causal existence and the truths;
the eighth is declared to have as its object the meaning of the realms, such as the past and so forth.
Indeed, for the sake of the ninth [category], the conditioned is apprehended as the supreme object;
this term "power" (bala) is dependent on two factors, but power itself consists in non-obstruction.
In every joint of the Buddha’s body, there is the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
moreover, that tangible quality is superior to the sevenfold strength of elephants and so forth.
The four forms of fearlessness arise from the complete attainment of one's own and others' welfare;
two have the nature of the first and last powers, while two are the functions of the [first] two knowledges.
The threefold application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthiti) depends upon the threefold assembly of listeners;
its specific characteristic is clear comprehension (saṃprajanya) whose capacity is established by recollection (saṃsmāra).
Because it consists of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it follows for a long time,
and because it functions equally toward all [beings], great compassion belongs only to one who is bound [to cyclic existence].
Non-contention, the knowledge resulting from prayer, and the four analytical knowledges—these five belong to the continuum of an Arhat; however, they are the ultimate limit of cultivation.
The other qualities, such as heedfulness and so forth, are common to all.
Listen as I shall describe the characteristics of these [qualities] as they have been taught.

The absence of conflict (araṇā) is conventional knowledge; it arises from a human being, relies upon the final dhyāna, occurs within the continuum of an Ārya, and perceives the objects of defilement along with their bases.
The knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*) is likewise supported by all phenomena;
it is declared to belong to one of unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*), and the same applies to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

The first [type of wisdom] is that which dispels confusion regarding the names associated with the intended meaning; the other is to be known as that which is manifested by it and which investigates through knowledge. *Abhidharmadīpa* 513.
The third is the refinement of words, which destroys delusion regarding knowledge;
the fourth, however, is the continuous discourse, which is oriented toward the production of meditative concentration and the like.
Indeed, that which is called "Meaning" (Arthākhyā) everywhere consists of six or nine knowledges;
likewise, that which is called "Inspiration" (Pratibhāna) consists of ten knowledges.
The analytical knowledge called "dharma" pertains to the desire realm and the dhyānas; the others, however, pertain to the first dhyāna and the desire realm.
These two analytical knowledges consist of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).

The supernormal powers consist of the direct realization of knowledge regarding: psychic power, the divine ear, the minds of others, former existences, death and rebirth, and the destruction [of the outflows]. Alternatively, they are sixfold, including the path of liberation. (Abhidharmadīpa 517)
The four [knowledges] are conventional knowledge; the five knowledges are the knowledge of the mind;
the supernormal knowledge of the destruction of all outflows consists of six knowledges, or alternatively, ten.
The sixth [knowledge] is present everywhere; the other five are in the fundamental stages of dhyāna.
They are acquired through effort or through detachment, and they have as their objects their own stage and the lower stages.
The three applications of mindfulness, the knowledge of the mental states of others,
and the supernormal powers of psychic power, the divine ear, and the divine eye are considered [to be] the first application of mindfulness.
The divine ear and eye are indeterminate (avyākṛta), while the others are considered auspicious;
they are supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) by virtue of being the fruit of supernormal knowledge, through the mental consciousness and wisdom (prajñā).
The three knowledges (*vidyā*) are considered to be for the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the three times;
one is [pure] by its very nature, being beyond training (*aśaikṣī*), while two arise from having that which is beyond training as their basis.
The supernormal power of the mind of psychic transformation and the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows are known as the three miracles.
Two of them remove [beings] from the grass-mats [of the world], while the supreme one removes them from the Māras.
Concentration is called "supernormal power" (ṛddhi); its fruit is the eightfold mastery.
This is twofold: movement and transformation; movement is held to be threefold.
The mind-made movement of the Teacher proceeds from his mere wish;
for others, it is produced by resolute conviction and thus carries along the body.
In the desire realm, the creation [of objects] is held to consist of visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects;
in the form realm, it is considered to consist of visible form and tangible objects, either within one's own body or externally.
However, those [attainments] are fourteen by means of the mind that is the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*).
Two are the fruits of the first dhyāna; from those, they increase by one for each successive higher stage.
The great gain [of the supernormal power of transformation] should be known as being like that of meditative absorption; it arises from the pure [attainment] and also spontaneously.
Emanation occurs by means of one's own level alone, though speech may also be produced by a lower level.
Except for the Sugata, these [emanations] speak only together with their creator;
when one speaks, all the emanated beings speak simultaneously.
Having empowered a transformation, they speak by means of another mind;
this empowerment applies even to that which is dead, provided it is a stable entity.
That which is won by many is unsurpassable; for the victor, it is the opposite.
That which arises from supernormal knowledge is indeterminate, but that which arises through rebirth is of three kinds.
This tenfold sovereignty of the Arhats arises from their possession of both the knowledge of the destruction of all outflows and liberation.
Even though such sovereignty is equal in this case for both teacher and disciple as described,
there is a very great difference in the Teacher, which has been explained previously.
Meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is the stability of the mind together with its factors; it is fourfold according to the distinction of its factors.
The designation "meditative absorption" applies directly (*āñjasī*) to that [state], while it is applied figuratively (*bhāktī*) to those things that coexist with it.
In brief, this fourfold class of meditative absorption has been explained;
I shall now describe its distinctions according to substance, in accordance with the scriptures.
Together with the four formless [attainments], meditative attainment is considered to be eightfold;
it is so designated because those [four] are spoken of as groups among the four and five aggregates, respectively.
When distinguished, however, the actual substances of the attainments are seventeen:
ten together with the eight preparatory stages (sāmantaka) and the intermediate dhyāna as well.
Indeed, these other distinctions as well will be explained as enjoined by the treatise;
yet all of them come within the range of the Buddha’s wisdom in their true nature.
The fundamental dhyānas are of three kinds, according to the distinctions of being "tasted" (sāsvāda) and so forth;
likewise, the three formless attainments (ārūpya) are so, while the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is considered to be of two kinds.
The neighboring [attainments] are of two kinds, seven in number; however, the first is considered to be of three kinds.
The intermediate dhyāna is likewise of three kinds; furthermore, that which is undefiled has a lower basis.

That which is accompanied by attachment and characterized by craving is considered mundane; that which is free from these [defilements] is supramundane and untainted (anāsrava). It is to be savored. Abhidh-d_541 //

In the first wholesome [dhyāna], there are five factors: applied thought (vitarka), mental subtlety (cittasūkṣmatā), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and concentration (samādhāna). The afflicted [dhyāna] is devoid of bliss.
In the second [dhyāna], there are four factors: internal serenity, bliss, joy, and concentration; however, in the defiled [state], these exist except for faith and bliss.
In the third and fifth [dhyānas], there are wisdom, mindfulness, equanimity, bliss, and stability.
However, in the defiled [dhyāna], it should be known that there are only two factors: concentration and the bliss of sensation.
In the final [dhyāna], there are four factors: two of equanimity, concentration, and mindfulness alone.
In the defiled fourth dhyāna, however, there are two factors: feeling and stability.
In terms of their substantial nature, there are eleven; by name, however, they are eight and ten.
These are called the limbs, and for this reason, they are traditionally known as the four categories (catuṣkoṭi).
And for calm abiding (śamatha),
there is no fixed establishment of factors (aṅga) in the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) of the dhyānas and the formless attainments (ārūpya).
Due to the destruction of applied and sustained thought, the cessation of inhalation and exhalation,
and the absence of the feeling of equanimity, the final [dhyāna] is called "unshakable" (ānejya).
In the first [dhyāna], there are joy, bliss, and equanimity; in the second, however, they exist with the exception of bliss;
in the third, there are bliss and equanimity; and in the last, only equanimity is recognized.
The visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses that produce informative intimation are likewise;
they belong to a level where there is no investigation (avicārā), and they are initially indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Drawn by the grasping of the sign of space, it is called the infinite mental application;
being devoid of all forms, it is the formless state known as the infinity of space.
Likewise, one who perceives the mastery of mind is characterized by the infinity of consciousness;
and one who is averse to the infinity of consciousness is called "nothingness."
Fearing the annihilation of that knowledge, one does not possess the notion of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception";
because it was practiced in such a manner from the beginning, it is designated by that name.

That mind which possesses vitarka and vicāra, which is dependent and accompanied by a subsequent [mental factor], and which takes the form of either the noble or the non-noble, is called the *anāgamya*.
Four types of meditators are proclaimed based on their insight into the four dhyānas:
those who understand the side of decline regarding the perception of prosperity and adversity, and so forth.
The meditator, the object of meditation, the act of meditation, and likewise the fruit of meditation—
because they would be subject to the aforementioned faults due to non-establishment, this tetrad beginning with the self does not exist.
Liberation results from the performance of ritual action as well as from the practice of knowledge;
for it exists when there is activity, even when there is the realization of reality as it truly is.
In this context, karma should be understood as twofold: meritorious action and non-meritorious action, as well as abstention from such actions.
Meritorious action is said to be threefold, and abstention is likewise described as being of that same kind.
But knowledge should be understood as that which is definitive, as previously illustrated;
he who resorts to anything other than this merely chews upon a bit of bridle.
Because they involve engaging in the infliction of suffering upon others, killing, greed, falsehood,
and so forth should be known as causes of the miserable realms (apāya) and as obstructions to the gateway of the highest good (śreya).

Because it enjoins the appropriate meaning, protects from suffering, and instructs regarding faults, it is called a "treatise" (śāstra); that which is otherwise should be known as the speech of a chatterer (vātika).

In some cases, the power of Pārasīka and other mantras is seen to be superior even to that of poison; however, this is not the case for all of them, because they do not avert misfortunes such as *ariṣṭa*.
The mind is defiled by passion and the like, and it is purified by faith and the like;
therefore, even for a brahmin, only one who possesses these qualities is liberated.
The pure [attainment] is of four kinds, beginning with that conducive to decline, respectively;
for it conforms to what is inferior, equal in strength, superior, and stainless.
Following the defilements, their own [level], the higher level, or the stainless [path],
there are respectively two, three, three, or two [moments] immediately after those belonging to the side of decline and so forth.
The leap-meditation (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) belongs to an Arhat of immovable nature (akopyadharman).
Its preparatory practice (prayoga) is twofold, performed with the desire to conquer by going and returning through the stages (bhūmi).
By skipping stages of the dharma-ground, one attains the eight [levels] from the so-called pure [attainment] as the uncontaminated;
from the pure [attainment], one attains its own third [level]; and from the pure, the stainless is the culmination.
The pure existences of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the formless realms (ārūpya) arise only from their own level and those above it;
however, one situated at the peak of existence (bhavāgra), having no other destination, takes hold of the stainless [path] at the beginning.
Upon the attainment of the first dhyāna by a fool (bāla) and others, there is only mundane cultivation (bhāvanā);
this also applies when the intermediate dhyāna has not been attained and has arisen [only] excluding the stages of heat (ūṣman) and so forth.
For one who is free from passion, it is likewise when the preceding neighboring stage has not been attained;
however, for one who is detached from the preceding stage, there is the cultivation of that which is indeed stainless.
In the subsequent knowledge of the path of certainty, in the increase of the faculties of one in training,
in the path called "uninterrupted," and in the path of seeing, there are twelve moments.
And in the detachment from the peak of existence (bhavāgra), excluding the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), [there is] the unshakable (ākopyā) ... // Abhidh-d_572 //
In the noble one’s detachment from desire, on the final path of liberation,
in the three knowledges called the "threefold," and in the attainment (nyāma) excluding the preparatory stage (anāgamya).

In the case of a learner (śaikṣa) who still possesses passion, when increasing the faculties (indriya) belonging to the three lower realms, as well as in the paths of preparation (prayoga-mārga) and liberation (vimukti-mārga), and for those born from the desire realm up to the dhyānas; Abhidh-d_574.
In the attainment of the two kinds of arhatship on the final path of liberation,
and for those learners who are detached in the conquest of the other three realms without distraction.
The cultivation of both [types] does not occur in either case;
rather, the entry into the state of certainty (nyāma) occurs upon the basis of the *anāgamya* stage, during the arising of the factors conducive to that [certainty], and so forth.

In the second [moment] and those following, one should infer by means of this very same method through reasoning; thus, the cultivation of future [moments] should be understood within the knowledge of the principles of the Abhidharma.
The wholesome fundamental dhyānas, when accompanied by relish, have their own level as their object; for one with universal vision, they are wholesome.
The fundamental formless attainments are wholesome and do not take lower realms as their objects.
The mental impurities are abandoned by means of the pure meditations and formless attainments;
however, those of the lower stages are acquired even by the neighboring pure states.
The three types of meditative absorption (samādhi), beginning with those accompanied by applied and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra), have been explained.
That [state] is characterized by duality in the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), whereas elsewhere it is without duality.
The other three concentrations, beginning with emptiness, are both with outflows and without outflows; they pertain to eleven stages and illuminate the aspects of the noble ones.
The ten aspects of the wishless are considered to be two types of emptiness;
the signless proceeds by means of the four aspects of the deathless.
Furthermore, for the sake of attaining the two kinds of liberation,
those same three stainless [factors] are revealed by the term "gateways to liberation" (vimokṣamukha).
The three [meditations] called "subsequent concentrations," beginning with the emptiness of emptiness,
take as their objects two things— the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)— by way of emptiness and likewise by way of impermanence.
The last [attainment] grasps cessation known as non-analytical (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as peaceful;
all eleven stages are with outflows (*sāsrava*), occurring among humans, and are not subject to anger.
The cultivation of concentration through dhyāna is the first pure [state] for the sake of happiness;
the supernormal power of the eye is said to be for the sake of vision; and those [cultivations] involving effort are for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.
That which is the final [path] in the diamond-like meditative absorption (vajropama-dhyāna) for the sake of the destruction of all afflictions—
this very sutra was proclaimed by the Buddha as being applicable to himself.
Among the four immeasurables, loving-kindness is non-hatred, as is compassion;
sympathetic joy is a form of gladness, while equanimity is held to be non-attachment.
This is declared to be the antidote for ill-will, cruelty, lack of delight, thirst, and hatred, for the purpose of taming one's own mind.
Loving-kindness is pleasant in bestowing happiness; compassion is oriented toward the destruction of suffering;
sympathetic joy is inclined toward rejoicing; and the last [equanimity] is directed toward these very beings. (Abhidh-d 590)
Their mode of conduct is to be understood through the aspects such as being happy and so forth;
yet, by means of even one of these, one attains union with Brahman.
Among humans, the two meditations called *muditā* (sympathetic joy) have objects that are the desires [of beings];
others [the remaining four immeasurables] belong to six stages. Some, however, maintain that they exist in seven stages.
The eight liberations have been taught; among them, two consist of the nature of the foul.
These two occur in the first and last dhyānas, while the third is characterized by non-attachment.
The four wholesome formless states are called liberations when they are in a state of meditative concentration;
the attainment known as cessation is declared to be the eighth liberation.
Its manifestation occurs immediately after the extremely subtle [attainment].
Even the mind of emergence from this state is its own pure and stainless lower [level].
The first three liberations have as their objects things belonging to the desire realm that are visible;
the others, however, consist of the category of subsequent knowledge and observe the suffering and so forth of their own or higher realms.
In the Sūtra, a set of eight bases called the "perceptions of mastery" is taught;
this, functioning as a supplement to the liberations, demonstrates sovereignty over the mind.
